stories.title_en: Postgres 19 is late because so many more bugs are being found now

comments.author: BatteryMountain
comments.text:
This is a good thing. Repaying technical debt is always a great thing.
On our own 1.5M loc system, we've found and fixed thousands of bugs, security holes and circular dependencies in the last year. Code quality has increased, test coverage increased. We've also recently set our compiler to treat warnings as errors, and to be as strict as possible. It is absolutely amazing to see the gaps being filled, it would've been an impossible task for human devs and IDE's would've made it very uncomfortable. We've also ironed out all the bugs and failure modes in our infrastructure automation / monitoring. Our next project is to eliminate all 3rd party dependencies, and after that to rebuild our frontends completely using zero frameworks, not touching npm ever again after that.
So when I read this about postgres, I was very happy that they found and pursued this side quest. They can make the codebase bullet proof.

comments.author: CharlesW
comments.text:
>
This year is going to be different. PostgreSQL 19 most likely won’t be released until November… […] So, what happened? The short answer is that LLMs happened. […] There’s a huge amount of code, and that code contains a huge number of bugs. […] What’s different now is that it’s become vastly easier to find those bugs.

That it might disrupt the project's "traditional" release cadence a bit doesn't seem terribly bad in light of the alternative, which is shipping another major update with bugs which have apparently haunted the codebase for some time.

comments.text:
I did a little AI-assisted bug-hunting in Postgres this summer in between jobs, and the haul was staggering.  Multiple serialization anomalies (eg [0] [1] [2]), foreign key integrity issues ([3] [4]), planner correctness bugs such as [5]. Various CVE-worthy vulnerabilities. An unfixable timezone bug [6]. The list got so long that I had to triage what I even had time to report, and settled for a dozen or two out of hundreds of candidates. Now imagine the entire world doing this.

[1] Serializable anomaly: duplicate primary keys:
https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/CA+COZaBOiiRPmEfX...
[2] SERIALIZABLE can commit write skew after SSI summarization:
https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/CA+COZaCtK=UQbeQw...
[3] Fix temporal foreign key validation of pre-existing rows
https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/CA+COZaChq_ukm2o7...
[4] Lost lock during toasting allows FK violation
https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/CA+COZaC-2-GQabq+...
[5] Partition pruning can incorrectly exclude a RANGE default partition

stories.title_en: One-minute frequency disturbances from synchronization in power systems

comments.author: schiffern
comments.text:
The corresponding concept in gears is to avoid meshing two gears unless the number of teeth are co-prime, because this will cause uneven wear patterns. If the tooth counts are coprime, then each tooth will contact every tooth on the other gear the same number of times, effectively "wear leveling" the teeth.
In this instance, one fix is to fire the timer every 59.XXX seconds, so it will naturally drift out of phase with the minute hand of the clock.
If work needs to be done exactly every 60 seconds, this is fixed by having a WAIT(RAND(60e6)) microseconds during the first timer initialization, so if 10,000 units start simultaneously they don't try all at once. This is good practice in most (all?) systems. Hint: test power and infra outage/reconnect, which can unintentionally sync timers.
This is why many software will do automated updates every 17 hours: 17 is coprime with 24.
Classic "thundering herd" mitigation tactics.
Edit: Tempting to blame IoT, but (since this is news) I don't think anyone knew there was something to fix here. We have the tools however.

comments.author: kazinator
comments.text:
I'm skeptical that this one minute jitter period is solely attributable to one minute timers in power inverter equipment. It's likely the net scale effect of all cron-like scheduling of actions in everything with a microprocessor. All the long-term scheduling that is done with minute precision (i.e. seconds field is implicitly :00) regardless of its individual period.  Like if one device is scheduling at x:17 and x:47 every hour, another one is doing x:06, x:09, x:12, x:15, ... and numerous other combinations, at scale, the common divisor will be one minute. If wall clock time is used, all the devices that are synchronized to a network time will have cron-like scheduling events firing at xx:xx:00 for all values of x.
This type of scheduling should be randomized at the seconds level, perhaps. Unfortunately, it would require a massively coordinated effort across numerous operating system and application stacks.

Not sure why so many things use the compatibility form of normalisation.
Some older RFCs even recommended using it for passwords, which needlessly reduces entropy (yes we need to normalise passwords because of combining characters, but we don’t need to collapse symbols that a user can choose from, like ſ and s).
In my opinion, the compatibility form makes mostly sense for searching text, and even then it’s sometimes annoying (I want to search exactly for ss and not ß, browser). If you know of other good use cases let me know.
It also OK to disallow registering two identifiers with the same compatibility normalisation form (edit: this does not prevent all homoglyph attacks BTW, that is another can of worms), but I don’t see the need to normalise the identifier when it’s used.

comments.author: adrian_b
comments.text:
Unfortunately the article does not identify precisely the "miracle" wheat.
"Triticum turgidum" is ambiguous, because this wheat species has many different subspecies, with very different characteristics.
There are 2 important subspecies of "Triticum turgidum", emmer wheat, which was 1 of the 3 cereals domesticated at the beginning of the Neolithic (barley, einkorn wheat and emmer wheat), and durum wheat (a.k.a. pasta wheat or macaroni wheat), which was produced from emmer wheat by a genetic mutation, several thousand years after domestication.
From the article, it is not clear if the discussed wheat is just some cultivar of emmer wheat or it belongs to a more exotic subspecies of "Triticum turgidum".
Any references from the Bible are unlikely to describe anything else but some variety of emmer wheat.
While most wheat-based food is nowadays produced from either hexaploid bread wheat or tetraploid durum wheat, there are on the market various niche products (e.g. some kinds of biscuits) made from spelt wheat, emmer wheat or einkorn wheat (though the product labels frequently confuse the hexaploid spelt wheat with the tetraploid emmer wheat).
